body.text: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is making the right call in resisting a proposal by the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor (INSLM) to remove religious motivation from terrorism laws. The prime minister’s decision is based on the advice of the intelligence and policing agencies responsible for keeping Australians safe.

Before people start arguing that the government shouldn’t just give intelligence agencies what they want without checks and balances, they should remember that this decision doesn’t create more secret powers of surveillance. But it does ensure transparency for the public, and that’s the key reason for leaving the law as it is.
It is never easy for a government to reject a recommendation from a watchdog such as INSLM. After all, oversight is a vital part of Australia’s security architecture.

But this recommendation was not about oversight and accepting it would not have helped counter terrorism or strengthened social cohesion. According to The Australian, the INSLM’s Jake Blight has recommended that references to religious motivation be removed from Australia’s definition of terrorism and covered instead by the broader term of ideology.

Blight’s report, begun before the terror attack at Bondi, presumably will be his last before his term ends this month. INSLM’s job is to review and, where necessary, challenge our national security laws. This independent scrutiny ensures extraordinary powers on the books remain necessary, effective and proportionate. But INSLM’s recommendations must also withstand scrutiny, including from those with the responsibility for putting such laws into practice.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation have warned against the proposed change. So the question for government is clear. What problem is being solved by removing religious motivation that would outweigh recommendations of security agencies and the public’s need for transparency?

According to the government’s special envoy to combat Islamophobia, ‘removing religion as a motivating factor … is about ensuring that terrorism is defined by violent conduct and extremist ideology, not by religious identity’.

But reasons for rejection are clear. For a start, terrorism needs to be distinguished from other violent crimes. The definition in the Criminal Code does so by saying terrorism is serious violence or threats intended to advance a political, religious or ideological cause and intimidate the public or coerce governments. So it requires a specific ideology. If religious ideology were no longer part of the definition, how would the Bondi attack have been referred to?

It would have been unacceptable for authorities simply to refer to some kind of ideological attack without naming Islamic State. And they would still have needed to prove in court that there was some ideology, and in doing so they’d have to say it was religious. So, in an open court, the attempt to avoid the issue would fail.

There’s a different problem in a closed court: the public hears nothing about the motivation from the prosecutor and witnesses, and officials, guided by the intent of the legislative change, would probably keep religion out of public updates.

Yet the word still would get out through the media, and the public would be left with speculative and perhaps divisive suspicions. This would undermine social cohesion – doing the opposite of what Blight presumably intends. Removing religion from the law would say to the public that there is an institutional attempt to hide the truth from it. Openness about the motivation for terrorism helps societal response and repair.

And that has been the hallmark of Australia’s counter-terrorism policy. It includes publication of a terror threat level that informs Australians each day that there is a greater than 50 percent chance of an attack or attack planning in Australia. This knowledge has empowered the public and reassured it that governments and security agencies are working on the threat. The aim has been to ensure the public is alert, not alarmed.

Refusing to acknowledge religious ideology in terrorism is the opposite of such transparency. Indeed, religion is the most prevalent factor in Australia’s terrorism caseload. Removing the word from the definition would not suddenly reduce the number of religiously motivated cases ASIO needed to investigate. According to AFP data, religious motives featured in 58 percent of terrorism charges since 2020.
Ultimately, this is how representative democracy should work.

Independent reviewers examine the law, security agencies provide operational advice, elected governments decide, parliament acts as a check and the public can hold politicians accountable at elections. So we seem to have reached the right outcome by the right means. Yet there’s still an unnerving possibility to consider about INSLM’s proposal: would it have been rejected if it had been made before Bondi? Probably, but maybe not. What if the INSLM had made this proposal in the period between 2022 and 2024 in which the threat of terrorism was lowered? Might the perception of lower risk have made it seem safe to bow to political pressure to make the change?

We hope not. Our security laws should always be up for review but never be changed on the basis that a threat is considered low today. Threats such as terrorism, espionage or war are permanent, and so should be the protections and information available to the public.
This is a lightly edited version of an article originally published in The Australian.
